## THE CURRENT MAP
17:14/q01 How is the command to read introduced in the sentence? [ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ · grammar]
  17:14/q01/p1 An omitted saying introduces direct speech to the person. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī compare omitted speech in 40:46 and 3:106. Al-Ṭabarī identifies God as speaker and the angels' deed-register as object; al-Rāzī says God speaks through angels. Al-Samīn allows the clause to be adjectival or circumstantial; al-Ālūsī also allows an independent sentence. Ibn ʿĀshūr says context makes the speaker plain.
17:14/q02 How is the imperative ٱقْرَأْ formed or pronounced? [ٱقْرَأْ · readings]
  17:14/q02/p1 Its imperative drops the hamza's ḍamma; a light or replaced hamza is also reported. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās adduces Arab replacement of hamza and Zuhayr's line وإلا يبد بالظلم يظلم; Ibn al-Jawzī reports Abū Jaʿfar's light hamza.
17:14/q03 Can someone who was unable to read in life read the record then? [ٱقْرَأْ · interpretation]
  17:14/q03/p1 Yes; everyone reads the record at resurrection, including the formerly illiterate. — reasons: Qatāda is repeatedly transmitted; al-Ḥasan says literate and illiterate alike. Al-Biqāʿī says God grants the ability and each reads personally. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows miraculous understanding of inscriptions.
17:14/q04 What does reading one's book mean here? [ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether reading concerns a displayed register or the soul's disclosed knowledge.)
  17:14/q04/p1 The person reads or understands the displayed account of deeds. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls it the angels' counted register; Ibn ʿĀshūr says reading can mean knowledge of recorded deeds or miraculous understanding of writing. Al-Biqāʿī stresses personal reading rather than another reader. Al-Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī report that the person recalls every deed as if performing it then, explaining 18:49.
  17:14/q04/p2 The intellect reads the soul's exposed impressions when bodily attachment ends. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says each deed leaves a lasting effect, like water drops boring stone; conventional letters signify sounds by agreement, whereas soul impressions are intrinsic. He cites 50:22 and affirms outward reports as true too. Al-Ālūsī calls this remote from the plain sense; Asad reports al-Rāzī's allegory of complete recollection.
17:14/q05 Why command the person to read the record? [ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the imperative primarily elicits acknowledgment or sharpens rebuke.)
  17:14/q05/p1 It establishes proof by making the person recognize and confess the deeds, leaving no excuse. — reasons: Al-Māwardī says reading makes one acknowledge the deeds. Al-Jishumī says it completes proof and shows no injustice. Al-Ṭabrisī says every deed and recompense is seen. Ibn al-Jawzī adds that Hell follows sin while Paradise is grace. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a compelled challenge and says the person already knows the deeds.
  17:14/q05/p2 It heightens reproach and rebuke. — reasons: Al-Māwardī offers this as another purpose of making the person read.
17:14/q06 What is the person's book? [كِتَٰبَكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether 'book' denotes the written register, deeds themselves, or a figurative record within the person.)
  17:14/q06/p1 It is the complete record of the person's deeds, displayed at resurrection. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says recording angels keep and count it; al-Ḥasan's report says two noble angels write it, roll it at death, and place it around the neck until resurrection. Study Quran cites 82:10–12 and lists parallels 17:71, 18:49, 69:19, 69:25, 84:7, 84:10. Al-Biqāʿī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī say no deed is omitted; the latter says it was already prepared but is brought out from heedlessness.
  17:14/q06/p2 The book is the actual deeds and their revealed realities, rather than ordinary written signs. — reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 3:30 and 50:22: deeds themselves appear with consequences, and the clinging 'bird' and book name the same deed. Their exposure confirms unavoidable recompense and removes concealment.
  17:14/q06/p3 The book can be the soul inscribed with enduring traces of deeds. — reasons: Al-Rāzī likens habitual acts to drops wearing stone; soul impressions outlast conventional letters and become apparent on separation from the body. Study Quran reports this and cites bodily testimony at 24:24, 36:65, 41:20–22. Al-Ālūsī calls the reading remote but reports the view that outward and inward senses coexist. Al-Rāzī says the impressions reveal felicity or misery and explicitly affirms this spiritual sense alongside outward narrated events.
  17:14/q06/p4 The book can represent the person and full recollection of the past life. — reasons: Some commentators in Study Quran picture tongue as pen, saliva as ink, limbs as page and memory as dictated record; al-Qurṭubī gives tongue, saliva and limbs as a pious saying. Asad transmits al-Rāzī's allegory of complete comprehension, citing 37:19, 39:68 and 50:22.
17:14/q07 What does a report say happens when a believer receives and reads the book? [كِتَٰبَكَ · reports]
  17:14/q07/p1 A believer sees sins within and good deeds outside, then learns the sins were forgiven and rejoices. — reasons: Ubayy says the person led many to good, fears sins, finds them forgiven and good deeds doubled; his face brightens, he receives the book in his right hand, a crown, two garments, ornaments at every joint and Adam's sixty-cubit stature, then announces the reward to companions with 69:19–23. Bakr says the visible good deeds draw envy, and private forgiveness brings joy, citing 69:19 and, in al-Rāzī, 80:38–39. Al-Ālūsī's version begins with feared sins, then forgiven sins and increasing light and joy, citing 69:19–20.
17:14/q08 What does a report say happens when an unbeliever reads the book? [كِتَٰبَكَ · reports]
  17:14/q08/p1 The unbeliever sees good deeds rejected and then sins, with darkness and lament. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī's report cites 25:23 for rejected deeds and 69:25–26 for the lament.
17:14/q09 What is the grammatical subject of كَفَىٰ and the function of ب in بِنَفْسِكَ? [كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the bāʾ introduces the overt subject or belongs to a different analysis of kafā.)
  17:14/q09/p1 Nafsika is the subject in nominative position; bāʾ is added for emphasis. — reasons: Al-Farrāʾ says the bāʾ can be omitted with a raised noun in praise or blame, unlike ordinary verbs, and adduces كفى الهدي. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī cite poetry without bāʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 4:79. Al-Ālūsī calls this the majority parse.
  17:14/q09/p2 The subject is an implicit notion of sufficiency, so bāʾ is not extra. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn mention this analysis; al-Ālūsī includes it among alternatives. Al-Burhān supplies kāna after kafā, with bi-nafsika its predicate, or a pronoun explained by accusative ḥasīban as in نعم رجلا زيد.
  17:14/q09/p3 Kafā is an imperative-like form with an implicit addressee, and bāʾ is not extra. — reasons: Al-Samīn finds the analysis weak because kafā accepts verbal inflections; al-Ālūsī says the majority prefers the ordinary past-verb parse. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the indeclinable imperative-like meaning اكتف.
17:14/q10 Why is كَفَىٰ masculine although نَفْسِكَ is grammatically feminine? [كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether masculine agreement is allowed with the feminine noun nafs.)
  17:14/q10/p1 Masculine agreement is permitted because nafs is grammatically, not naturally, feminine. — reasons: Al-Samīn cites Qur'anic feminine agreement at 21:6 and 6:4 yet allows masculine for figurative gender; Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes the same point. Al-Ālūsī notes the difficulty and analogous verbs that do agree in feminine.
  17:14/q10/p2 The lack of feminine agreement argues that bāʾ is not extra and nafs is not the subject. — reasons: Al-Burhān reasons that if bāʾ were extra, kafā would agree with normally feminine nafs; he offers omitted kāna or an explanatory pronoun as parses.
17:14/q11 What does بِنَفْسِكَ refer to as the sufficient witness? [بِنَفْسِكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether self-witnessing is the person's direct knowledge or testimony of bodily members.)
  17:14/q11/p1 It means the person's own self and knowledge of the deeds. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent sense and notes Abū ʿUbayda's emphasis on what the person knows; Ibn Kathīr says the person remembers and knows no injustice or alien deed was recorded. Al-Ālūsī calls the bodily-limbs reading contrary to the apparent meaning.
  17:14/q11/p2 It means the person's bodily limbs testifying if the person denies. — reasons: Muqātil compares the denial in 6:23 and testimony in 75:14, specifying self, tongue, hands and feet. Al-Biqāʿī says the tongue may deny but limbs confirm the precise record. Abū Ḥayyān transmits Muqātil; al-Ālūsī objects that this departs from the apparent meaning.
17:14/q12 What does ٱلْيَوْمَ modify? [ٱلْيَوْمَ · grammar]
  17:14/q12/p1 It is the time adverb governed by kafā. — reasons: Al-Samīn gives the attachment; al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī call it the adverb.
17:14/q13 What does حَسِيبًا mean? [حَسِيبًا · meaning] (turns on: Whether ḥasīb is understood from counting and judgment or from sufficiency and testimony.)
  17:14/q13/p1 An accountant or reckoner who audits and calls to account. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba gives the active sense beside sufficient; al-Wāḥidī compares God's epithet in 33:39. Al-Zamakhsharī likens the form to occupational nouns; al-Kalbī and others give accountant or intensive reckoner. Al-Qurṭubī's pious saying pictures tongue as pen, saliva as ink and limbs as witnesses.
  17:14/q13/p2 A witness against oneself. — reasons: Muqātil says no better witness than oneself can be found; al-Zajjāj says the self suffices as witness. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī explain that a witness suffices a claimant in the matter at issue.
  17:14/q13/p3 One who suffices, standing in place of a witness or accountant. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba offers sufficient as an alternative to recko
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<17:14 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
ner; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī say the witness suffices the claimant. Al-Zajjāj allows non-Qur'anic feminine ḥasība.
17:14/q14 What is the syntactic role of حَسِيبًا? [حَسِيبًا · grammar] (turns on: Whether the accusative specifies the sufficiency or describes the person's state.)
  17:14/q14/p1 It is an accusative specification, clarifying how the self suffices. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj states tamyīz. Al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī also mention a circumstantial alternative; al-Sarrāj specifically posits an omitted subject for that parse.
  17:14/q14/p2 It is a circumstantial accusative. — reasons: Al-Naḥḥās allows ḥāl as well as specification; al-Ṭabrisī attributes this with an omitted subject to al-Sarrāj. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī report it too.
17:14/q15 Why is حَسِيبًا masculine with feminine نَفْس? [بِنَفْسِكَ حَسِيبًا · grammar] (turns on: Whether agreement follows the referent's sense or the noun's formal shape.)
  17:14/q15/p1 Nafs means a person, so the description follows the person's sense. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and others also point to male-associated roles such as witness, judge and trustee; al-Samīn cites a poem. Al-Bursawī takes nafs as person; al-Ālūsī also mentions the adjective pattern. Abū Isḥāq permits feminine ḥasība outside Qur'anic wording.
  17:14/q15/p2 Nafs lacks a visible feminine marker, allowing masculine description. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbārī compares sky and earth, citing 73:18; Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān cite poetry with masculine description of earth, including أبقل.
17:14/q16 How does عَلَيْكَ connect syntactically and semantically? [عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا · grammar] (turns on: Whether ḥasīb is construed as an accountant or a sufficient witness.)
  17:14/q16/p1 It depends on the sense of ḥasīb as one who reckons against a person. — reasons: Al-Nasafī cites the idiom 'reckoned this against him'; al-Samīn cites al-Zamakhsharī and examples from Sībawayh; al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī agree. Ibn ʿĀshūr says ʿalayka implies testimony against the person.
  17:14/q16/p2 It marks the matter about which a sufficient witness answers the claimant. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn give the witness construction as an alternative.
17:14/q17 What does it mean that the person suffices as their own reckoner? [كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the sufficient self-testimony is direct self-accounting or bodily testimony.)
  17:14/q17/p1 One's own knowledge, record and confession suffice to account for and judge one's deeds, proving the judgment fair. — reasons: Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī say no outside witness or recorder is needed; al-Ḥasan repeatedly calls this justice. Al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Bursawī say it removes excuses and establishes proof. Ibn Kathīr says the person remembers the deeds and no alien deed appears; Ibn al-Jawzī contrasts Paradise by grace and Hell by sin. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 66:7 for unavoidable evidence.
  17:14/q17/p2 The person's own limbs testify when the tongue denies the deeds. — reasons: Muqātil illustrates this through 6:23 and 75:14; al-Biqāʿī says the record omits nothing and limbs answer denial.
17:14/q18 Who is addressed by the command? [ٱقْرَأْ بِنَفْسِكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether a specific report about an unbeliever limits the general address.)
  17:14/q18/p1 Every person, believer and unbeliever, faces the command and account. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects restricting it to unbelievers merely because al-Suddī tells an unbeliever's story. Ibn ʿĀshūr points back to the person in 17:13; the believer and unbeliever reports cover both.
  17:14/q18/p2 In al-Suddī's reported episode, an unbeliever asks to audit himself and is told to read. — reasons: The unbeliever invokes God's declaration that He is not unjust to servants. Al-Ālūsī says this episode does not limit the verse's general address.
17:14/q19 What afterlife events does this verse establish? [* · interpretation]
  17:14/q19/p1 There will be a record, resurrection, precise reckoning and just recompense for one's own deeds. — reasons: Al-Jishumī explicitly names afterlife reckoning and records. Al-Ṭabarī says angels keep the register; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses exhaustive knowledge. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says deeds cling to their doer and their consequences inevitably appear. Iṣlāḥī says nobody bears another's burden; Kuranyolu says each sees the result; Study Quran cites 3:117, 10:44 and 29:40 for people wronging themselves.
17:14/q20 What does the command imply about who creates the act of reading? [ٱقْرَأْ · theology]
  17:14/q20/p1 The command would lose its function if God created the person's act of reading. — reasons: Al-Jishumī uses the imperative itself against the doctrine that God creates the commanded act.
17:14/q21 What does self-accounting imply for responsibility and divine justice? [كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ حَسِيبًا · theology]
  17:14/q21/p1 People are accountable for their deeds; reckoning proves God does not wrong them. — reasons: Al-Jishumī argues that determinism would make God accountable for the deed, and that creating disbelief while preventing faith would make accounting pointless and unjust. Al-Bursawī says the person's own confession establishes proof. Study Quran says actions lead to salvation or condemnation, while mercy remains beyond calculation.
17:14/q22 How should people prepare now for this self-accounting? [بِنَفْسِكَ حَسِيبًا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the practical counsel concerns reviewing deeds or prioritizing current acts.)
  17:14/q22/p1 Audit and weigh one's deeds before the final presentation while amendment is possible. — reasons: ʿUmar's repeated counsel adds preparing for the great presentation; al-Bursawī stresses that tomorrow offers no repair. Al-Ḥasan urges a sound answer to questioning or a shroud for the Fire. Al-Sulamī contrasts righteous people reckoned now with wicked people reckoned later. Elmalılı urges daily examination. A Kashf al-Asrār report's king makes his self recount each evening's words, deeds, movements and stillness, which it finds hard to bear even for one day.
  17:14/q22/p2 In choosing among worthy acts, perform the one nearer to and weightier with God first. — reasons: Sahl's context concerns duties, sunnas and voluntary acts; Tustarī presents this as practical self-accounting.
17:14/q23 Where does self-accounting take place? [بِنَفْسِكَ حَسِيبًا · interpretation]
  17:14/q23/p1 It may be private between servant and God or public between the person and others. — reasons: Sahl gives both spheres as forms of self-accounting.
17:14/q24 Why can a person be said to have authored their book? [كِتَٰبَكَ · interpretation]
  17:14/q24/p1 The person's own acts dictated its contents. — reasons: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says people should read the book because they themselves dictated it; Study Quran's reported image makes memory dictate the record while tongue, saliva and limbs form its writing implements.
17:14/q25 How does this account connect with the preceding passage? [* · links] (turns on: Which preceding theme supplies the transition to each person's record and judgment.)
  17:14/q25/p1 Revelation and warning have supplied proof, leaving no excuse when records are judged. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says the completed account of signs and warning leads to the record; al-Ālūsī relays his proof of oneness, prophethood and resurrection. Kuranyolu likewise connects revelation, faith, reward and punishment to responsibility.
  17:14/q25/p2 God's worldly and religious benefits call for obedience, which is then examined. — reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī give this as a second link.
  17:14/q25/p3 Creation is for worship, and the sun, moon, night and day aid obedience that judgment assesses. — reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī cite 51:56; the latter says judgment asks whether people obeyed or rebelled.
  17:14/q25/p4 The passage moves from God's guidance-book to the person's exhaustive deed-book. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī cites 18:49: the personal book shows whether the first book was followed.
  17:14/q25/p5 The precise personal record makes the preceding general declaration of God's knowledge concrete. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr links encouragement and warning to 17:9–12, saying specific human deeds follow the general 'everything' for emphasis.
  17:14/q25/p6 Human haste and desire in the surrounding rebuke explain why the enduring deed-record must be reviewed. — reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī says people confuse benefit and harm and pursue desires though every act remains with its doer.
  17:14/q25/p7 The larger section calls Jews and Quraysh to the straight path and contrasts acceptance with rejection. — reasons: Iṣlāḥī says it rebukes demands for punishment by people blind to signs and alludes to God's treatment of nations.
17:14/q26 How does this verse illustrate the seven revealed modes in a reported classification? [* · sciences]
  17:14/q26/p1 It exemplifies the mode concerning resurrection and accounting. — reasons: Al-Burhān reports a ninth explanation of the seven modes as knowledge types: creation, unity, transcendence, attributes, commands, mercy and punishment, resurrection and accounting, and prophethood; it gives this verse as the accounting example. Al-Qāḍī says all seven noncontradictory transmitted modes entered the codex except nonmutawātir material; al-Ṭabarī and most later scholars favored one, al-Shāṭibī distinguished Abū Bakr's and ʿUthmān's compilations, and al-Ṭaḥāwī viewed the modes as temporary recitation ease.
17:14/q27 What related reading and syntax issues are reported for the preceding verse? [* · readings] (turns on: The two notes treat distinct issues in the preceding verse.)
  17:14/q27/p1 The doubled laqqā governs two objects, and its passive leaves one as subject and one as object. — reasons: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī gives the transitivity and passive parse.
  17:14/q27/p2 Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the qāf with imāla, while the unchanged vowel is also acceptable. — reasons: Al-Fārisī accepts both pro

nunciations.
17:14/q28 What ancillary rhetorical observations are included among the source notes? [* · rhetoric] (turns on: The notes discuss separate rhetorical examples alongside the verse.)
  17:14/q28/p1 Verb-first interrogation can deny the action's occurrence or propriety. — reasons: Al-Jurjānī says such a question may challenge an impossible boast or condemn a proposal; 11:28 illustrates the latter. A figurative impossible-act question compares boast or hope to absurdity rather than asserting literal expectation.
  17:14/q28/p2 Noun-first interrogation directs doubt to the alleged actor's identity or capacity. — reasons: Al-Jurjānī distinguishes it from action-focused questioning. In 'Would he kill me while the sword is beside me?', the sword is an impediment even though the actor could kill.
  17:14/q28/p3 The aim of such interrogatives is to make the listener reconsider, feel shame, desist or fall silent. — reasons: Al-Jurjānī treats 'denial' as a label for this effect.
  17:14/q28/p4 A cited Bedouin couplet and related images are praised for their figurative force. — reasons: Al-Jurjānī singles out خسأت, says dawn 'permits' sight because daylight removes night's hindrance, praises the al-Jāḥiẓ couplet and Bashshār's boil image, and finds 'toil as bridge to comfort' stronger than another bridge use, also citing Rabīʿa al-Raqqī.

## THE NEW NOTES
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p184/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | نستنسخ can mean copy, as يستسخر means mock, or solicit a record by ordering angels to write and preserve deeds; the cited verses show deeds are recorded and counted.

item.text: The new note supports the existing position that the book is a record of deeds. It adds al-Fārisī’s explanation of how angels write and preserve that record.
